newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam opens assembly session with list of woes.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam opens assembly session with list of woes.

text.p: Vietnam opened a critical session of its National Assembly on Tuesday with an unusually frank prime ministerial address cataloguing a range of problems afflicting economic development.
In a lengthy opening speech, Vo Van Kiet, considered a champion of reforms launched in the late 1980s, outlined the achievements of the past nine months and targets for the next five years.

But in contrast to the picture of gleaming socialist achievement normally reported on such occasions, Kiet listed a range of woes as the assembled deputies, leaders, diplomats and journalists sat in silence.

He stressed the need for coupling economic development with social order, security and discipline, and said corruption, incompetence, rural underemployment, vice, a trade deficit, slipping production levels and deflation had become serious concerns.
"In a nutshell, the government thinks these shortcomings could have been limited or overcome earlier," he said.
"All of these things have limited the achievements and results and caused psychological disadvantages for the effective mobilisation of production and business."

But the downbeat tone of Kiet's address was not reflected as strongly in views expressed later as delegates and guests paused for a break in the gardens outside Ba Dinh Hall, the monolithic assembly venue.

A characteristically ebulient Communist Party Secretary-General Do Muoi spoke at length amid a posse of journalists about Hanoi's commitment to economic reforms, the fight against corruption and the need to overcome poverty.

General Vo Nguyen Giap, 84, -- military mastermind behind Vietnam's defeat of both the French and Americans and a key proponent of Vietnam's reform process -- conceded meanwhile there were problems but cautioned against reading too much into the picture of a downturn.
"Development never follows a straight line," he told Reuters. "We will face many difficulties and sometimes stagnancy... But as I said, in general the Vietnamese people will continue going forward."
Vietnam's National Assembly is due, over the next month, to discuss budgetary issues, tax proposals and approve a cabinet reshuffle as well as laws on legal documents and foreign investment.
The meeting is accorded added significance because of its proximity to a major Communist Party Congress held in late June -- a key policy-defining event.

Western economists say that despite problems with a yawning trade gap and a current account deficit put at up to 15 percent of gross domestic product, growth at around nine percent per annum remains steady and inflation, now at below three percent, has been kept under control.
Since reforms and an open-door policy were introduced 10 years ago Vietnam has witnessed an economic lift-off going from boom to boom.
However critics within the ruling Communist Party say social problems such as corruption and declining morals are on the rise and have called for measures aimed at ensuring tighter state control.
